bibl.title: Role of the Hippocampus in Distinct Memory Traces: Timing of Match and Mismatch Enhancement Revealed by Intracranial Recording

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the timing of goal-match and perceptual-mismatch signals in the human hippocampus during a working memory task
span.quote: However, the timing information in this process is unknown.

span.label: if and how the hippocampus is involved in working memory, and whether its components separate in time
span.quote: It is still unclear if and how the hippocampus is involved in working memory.

span.label: separates goal-match from perceptual-mismatch enhancement within identical stimuli and times them, finding mismatch about 150 ms earlier and localised bilaterally where match is left posterior
span.quote: We also found that this effect happened within 520 ms to 735 ms after the probe onset, ~150 ms later than the perceptual mismatch enhancement found bilaterally in both the anterior and posterior hippocampus.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We also found that this effect happened within 520 ms to 735 ms after the probe onset, ~150 ms later than the perceptual mismatch enhancement found bilaterally in both the anterior and posterior hippocampus.

span.label: hippocampal match and mismatch enhancement in working memory
span.quote: Emerging evidence has revealed that, within the hippocampus, neurons discriminate between novel and familiar stimuli through a firing rate increase to previously encountered stimuli (match enhancement), or through a firing rate increase to novel stimuli (mismatch enhancement) [ 17 – 19 ].

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Intracranial field potentials were recorded from 120 depth electrode contacts implanted in 8 human epilepsy patients who suffered from pharmaco-resistant epilepsy in Xuanwu Hospital (5 male, 3 female).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: whether an incoming event matches or mismatches expectation drives the hippocampus to switch between memory encoding and memory retrieval modes
span.quote: Whether the incoming events match or mismatch what we expect can influence the ability of the hippocampus to switch between memory encoding and retrieval modes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: decoding of task demand was degraded because participants defaulted to maintaining the sample in both tasks instead of simulating a new scene on switch trials, so the two tasks engaged more similar mental operations than the design intended
span.quote: Rather than maintaining the sample when it was the match task and simulating a new scenario when it was the switch task, the participant tended to maintain the sample no matter what the task was, which may lead to a poor performance in decoding.

span.label: the same probe display is a goal match or a perceptual match depending only on a verbal instruction, which dissociates the two within identical stimuli
span.quote: Thus, there were 4 possible object configurations in the Probe display: 1, the same objects at the same locations, called BOTH in the match task (correct response for this trial is ‘yes’) or PERCEPT in the switch task (correct response is ‘no’); 2, the same objects but switched locations, called NEITHER in the match task (correct response is ‘no’) or GOAL in the switch task (correct response is ‘yes’); 3, the same objects, with one in a new location, called LOC in both tasks (correct response is ‘no’); 4, the same locations, but one object is replaced by a new one, called OBJ in both tasks (correct response is also ‘no’). The last two conditions were designed for control purposes.

span.label: this is exactly what the earlier imaging work could not do, and the paper says why
span.quote: An event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging study has revealed enhanced hippocampal activation for images that match a maintained goal. However, due to the task, mixing perceptual-mismatches with goal-matches is inevitable

span.label: a two-step contrast is used: first find where the two instruction conditions differ, then ask within that window which of the two enhancement patterns holds
span.quote: If at least 10 ms consecutive time points of the t -test trace crossed the significance threshold of 0.05, and GOAL > PERCEPT, that time window was defined as a potential significant interval.

span.label: latencies are validated against 1000 label permutations rather than taken from the contrast alone
span.quote: We checked the statistical significance of these effects through Monte Carlo permutations.

span.label: the identical electrode configuration across patients is what makes grand averaging across individuals defensible
span.quote: This electrode configuration was used for every patient and allowed us to collect neuronal response data from the same (or at least similar) brain region, with the same electrode order across patients, making grand average of event-related potentials (ERPs) possible

span.label: patients with hippocampal sclerosis are excluded so that the recorded tissue is morphologically intact
span.quote: We included only patients with a depth electrode in a morphologically intact hippocampus (as defined by MRI).

span.label: display timings were shortened because the constraint that set them belonged to a method this study does not use
span.quote: The durations of the displays and intervals used in the current version were also much shorter than those used in the original task because the temporal restrictions imposed by the use of fMRI were not present in our intracranial EEG experiment.

span.label: the task was modified to fit the patients rather than the patients excluded to fit the task, which is disclosed
span.quote: The major difference between this modified version of the match or switch task and the original task was the repeated presentation of the sample after the auditory instruction (sample repetition) (Fig. 2 ). This modification was implemented to aid patient performance because, in general, their memory performance was impaired compared to normal participants, and they had difficulty performing the original version of the task.

span.label: the single-participant threshold is loosened relative to the group analysis, and the loosening is stated
span.quote: In this single participant level test, we slightly loosened the constraint defining a significant interval from continuous 10 ms to 5 ms.

span.label: single-trial decoding is used to ask whether task demand is recoverable at all, independently of the averaged contrasts
span.quote: We used a statistical learning approach [ 34 ] to quantify whether the information from IFPs available in single trials was sufficient to distinguish whether it is memory maintenance (match task) or simulation of a specific future event (switch task).

span.label: the decoding result is then argued to be an underestimate, because subjects probably maintained the sample regardless of instruction
span.quote: The result of the decoding might be compromised, because the dissociation between the switch and match task relies on a different mental manipulation. Rather than maintaining the sample when it was the match task and simulating a new scenario when it was the switch task, the participant tended to maintain the sample no matter what the task was, which may lead to a poor performance in decoding.

span.label: The single-trial decoding result may be weakened because participants tended to maintain the sample regardless of which task was instructed.
span.quote: The result of the decoding might be compromised, because the dissociation between the switch and match task relies on a different mental manipulation.

span.label: The task had to be modified from the original because the epilepsy patients' memory performance was impaired relative to healthy participants.
span.quote: This modification was implemented to aid patient performance because, in general, their memory performance was impaired compared to normal participants, and they had difficulty performing the original version of the task.

span.label: the decoding may understate the effect because participants likely maintained the sample whatever the task
span.quote: The result of the decoding might be compromised, because the dissociation between the switch and match task relies on a different mental manipulation. Rather than maintaining the sample when it was the match task and simulating a new scenario when it was the switch task, the participant tended to maintain the sample no matter what the task was, which may lead to a poor performance in decoding.

span.label: the paradigm was altered from the original to make it performable by patients
span.quote: The major difference between this modified version of the match or switch task and the original task was the repeated presentation of the sample after the auditory instruction (sample repetition) (Fig. 2 ). This modification was implemented to aid patient performance because, in general, their memory performance was impaired compared to normal participants, and they had difficulty performing the original version of the task.

span.label: electrode placement was dictated entirely by clinical need
span.quote: The electrode locations were based exclusively on clinical criteria.

span.label: the task inseparably combines object identity with location, so the hippocampal involvement cannot be attributed to either alone
span.quote: It should also be noted that in the current paradigm (derived from Duncan [ 29 ]), a combination of two streams of information, object identity and position, are involved in the task. Even without the trial-by-trial changes in task requirement, increasing numbers of studies have revealed that multiple features and combinations of features in working memory activate the hippocampus

span.label: the supporting spatial-memory literature comes mostly from animal models
span.quote: The convergence to binding with locations in the current data and previous studies [ 13 ] consists of the well understood role of hippocampus in spatial memory and navigation (see [ 42 ] for a review), though animal models were used in most of the studies.

span.label: testing patients before and after resection is proposed as the missing comparison
span.quote: It will be of interest to test the results from the animal models on epilepsy patients before and after resection and to extend our understanding of the role of the hippocampus in different components of working memory and their interactions.

span.label: the dissociation between repetition suppression and sample-matched enhancement, imported as the template for what to look for in human hippocampus
span.quote: This revealed that in the perirhinal cortex some neurons are suppressed by any picture repetition, regardless of relevance, whereas others are enhanced, but only when a picture matches the sample

span.label: linear discriminant analysis after principal component reduction, used to ask whether the task instruction is recoverable from a single trial
span.quote: We used a statistical learning approach [ 34 ] to quantify whether the information from IFPs available in single trials was sufficient to distinguish whether it is memory maintenance (match task) or simulation of a specific future event (switch task).

span.label: working memory - as measured by a digit span, where these patients are intact, versus as measured by feature integration, where they are impaired; the same patients on two tests
span.quote: This is also consistent with the results of Piekema et al . [ 13 ] who showed that working memory in patients with medial temporal lobe epilepsy decreases when the integration of different features is required. However, if evaluated by the traditional digital memory span test, their working memory seems to be intact.

span.label: match enhancement - as a response to a goal state versus as a response to a previously perceived stimulus; the paradigm separates them within identical displays
span.quote: Thus, there were 4 possible object configurations in the Probe display: 1, the same objects at the same locations, called BOTH in the match task (correct response for this trial is ‘yes’) or PERCEPT in the switch task (correct response is ‘no’); 2, the same objects but switched locations, called NEITHER in the match task (correct response is ‘no’) or GOAL in the switch task (correct response is ‘yes’); 3, the same objects, with one in a new location, called LOC in both tasks (correct response is ‘no’); 4, the same locations, but one object is replaced by a new one, called OBJ in both tasks (correct response is also ‘no’). The last two conditions were designed for control purposes.

span.label: the same probe display - counting as GOAL or PERCEPT depending only on the verbal instruction that preceded it
span.quote: A modified version of the delayed-match-to-sample task was used. This paradigm dissociates goal match/mismatch from perceptual match/mismatch.

span.label: enhancement - a match effect where BOTH exceeds NEITHER, against a mismatch effect where NEITHER exceeds BOTH; two opposite orderings of the same four conditions
span.quote: A perceptually driven mismatch enhancement was revealed bilaterally in the hippocampus including both the anterior and posterior areas (electrode contacts #1, #2, #3, #4 and #9, #10, #11, #12). This enhancement effect occurred at different intervals on different electrode contacts, averaging from 376 ms to 555 ms (Fig. 4 ).

span.label: a late perceptual match effect that fits neither pattern cleanly, with BOTH above NEITHER but GOAL below PERCEPT
span.quote: A late perceptual match enhancement was found on electrodes #2 and #3 with a latency of 717 ms and 900 ms, which fitted a pattern of BOTH > NEITHER and GOAL < PERCEPT.

span.label: hippocampal role - as long-term declarative memory only, versus as also serving working memory encoding and retrieval
span.quote: Nevertheless, examination of the different forms of working memory in detail revealed that working memory is not affected by temporal lobectomy [ 7 ]. These results indicate that the role and different components of working memory may show different effects in the hippocampus or in its different sub-regions.

span.label: replicates → Duncan et al.'s fMRI dissociation of goal match and perceptual mismatch enhancement (reference [29])
span.quote: Consistent with our proposal and a previous study [ 29 ], we found goal match enhancement at electrode contacts #3 and #4, which were located on the left posterior hippocampus, and perceptual mismatch enhancement at electrode contacts #1, #2, #3, #4, and #9, #10, #11, #12, which included the anterior and posterior hippocampi bilaterally.

span.label: builds-on → Duncan (reference [29]) - stimuli and task design reused
span.quote: Stimuli were identical to those used by Duncan [ 29 ].

span.label: extends → previous electrophysiological research on match and mismatch enhancement (references [18], [19])
span.quote: The dissociation of different components of working memory at hippocampus revealed more information beyond previous electrophysiological research [ 18 , 19 ], demonstrating that match enhancement is more related with goal match at the hippocampus and mismatch enhancement is more related with perceptual mismatch.

span.label: extends → the fMRI study proposing parallel goal-match and perceptual-mismatch traces, by adding the timing it could not resolve
span.quote: A previous functional magnetic resonance imaging study reported evidence for parallel memory traces in the hippocampus: a controlled match signal detecting matches to internally-generated goal states and an automatic mismatch signal identifying unpredicted perceptual novelty.

span.label: critiques → earlier imaging designs in which perceptual mismatches and goal matches are unavoidably mixed
span.quote: An event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging study has revealed enhanced hippocampal activation for images that match a maintained goal. However, due to the task, mixing perceptual-mismatches with goal-matches is inevitable

span.label: contradicts → the traditional view that the hippocampus subserves long-term declarative memory only
span.quote: Nevertheless, examination of the different forms of working memory in detail revealed that working memory is not affected by temporal lobectomy [ 7 ]. These results indicate that the role and different components of working memory may show different effects in the hippocampus or in its different sub-regions.

span.label: builds-on → Miller and Desimone, who dissociated repetition suppression from sample-specific match enhancement in perirhinal cortex
span.quote: This revealed that in the perirhinal cortex some neurons are suppressed by any picture repetition, regardless of relevance, whereas others are enhanced, but only when a picture matches the sample

span.label: supports → evidence that the hippocampus is engaged when features must be bound to location but not for single features
span.quote: Finke et al . found that MTL lesions selectively reduce color-location associations, while color-only or location-only working memory is retained

span.label: extends → fMRI work that found only a subtle perceptual mismatch effect, by resolving it with intracranial timing
span.quote: This result showed the advantage of our approach in exploring the perceptual mismatch enhancement compared with the fact that fMRI research only found a subtle effect.

span.label: goal match enhancement —contrasted-with→ perceptual mismatch enhancement
span.quote: We also found that this effect happened within 520 ms to 735 ms after the probe onset, ~150 ms later than the perceptual mismatch enhancement found bilaterally in both the anterior and posterior hippocampus.

span.label: match enhancement —contrasted-with→ mismatch enhancement
span.quote: Emerging evidence has revealed that, within the hippocampus, neurons discriminate between novel and familiar stimuli through a firing rate increase to previously encountered stimuli (match enhancement), or through a firing rate increase to novel stimuli (mismatch enhancement)

span.label: working memory —operationalised-as→ delayed-match-to-sample
span.quote: A modified version of the delayed-match-to-sample task was used. This paradigm dissociates goal match/mismatch from perceptual match/mismatch.

span.label: left posterior hippocampus —part-of→ hippocampus
span.quote: This electrode configuration was used for every patient and allowed us to collect neuronal response data from the same (or at least similar) brain region, with the same electrode order across patients, making grand average of event-related potentials (ERPs) possible

span.label: intracranial field potential —operationalised-as→ linear discriminant analysis
span.quote: We used a statistical learning approach [ 34 ] to quantify whether the information from IFPs available in single trials was sufficient to distinguish whether it is memory maintenance (match task) or simulation of a specific future event (switch task).

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: Paired sample t tests revealed that the responses in the match task were faster than those in the switch task

span.label: t-test (sample-by-sample, time-resolved)
span.quote: The sample-by-sample t -test gave a time-resolved significance level for whether the local field potential (LFP) values differed across conditions.

span.label: ANOVA (two-way)
span.quote: To further confirm the existence of enhancement patterns, a sample-by-sample two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to the four ERPs (BOTH, GOAL, NEITHER and PERCEPT) during the defined goal match enhancement interval or perceptual mismatch enhancement interval.

span.label: permutation test
span.quote: We checked the statistical significance of these effects through Monte Carlo permutations.

span.label: ANOVA (three-way) with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons
span.term: ANOVA (three-way) with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: we conducted a multiple comparison of three-way ANOVA analysis with Bonferroni confidence interval adjustment

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement effect found in the right posterior hippocampus was significantly correlated with the accuracy of memory performance

span.label: linear discriminant analysis with principal component analysis
span.term: linear discriminant analysis with principal component analysis
span.quote: A linear discriminant analysis was performed with the principal component analysis approach for dimensionality reduction in the classification.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Numbers in parentheses represent standard error of the mean.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: For each electrode and each significant effect, the probability of the observed latency was <0.05.

span.label: sample-by-sample t -test
span.quote: If at least 10 ms consecutive time points of the t -test trace crossed the significance threshold of 0.05, and GOAL > PERCEPT, that time window was defined as a potential significant interval.

span.label: Monte Carlo permutations
span.quote: We checked the statistical significance of these effects through Monte Carlo permutations.

span.label: linear discriminant analysis
span.quote: We used a statistical learning approach [ 34 ] to quantify whether the information from IFPs available in single trials was sufficient to distinguish whether it is memory maintenance (match task) or simulation of a specific future event (switch task).

span.label: Bonferroni confidence interval adjustment
span.quote: For each electrode and each significant effect, the probability of the observed latency was <0.05.

span.label: Goal match enhancement appeared only at contacts in the left posterior hippocampus, whereas perceptual mismatch enhancement appeared bilaterally across both anterior and posterior hippocampus.
span.quote: Consistent with our proposal and a previous study [ 29 ], we found goal match enhancement at electrode contacts #3 and #4, which were located on the left posterior hippocampus, and perceptual mismatch enhancement at electrode contacts #1, #2, #3, #4, and #9, #10, #11, #12, which included the anterior and posterior hippocampi bilaterally.

span.label: The perceptual mismatch signal began before the goal match signal in every one of the eight participants.
span.quote: The perceptual mismatch enhancement began earlier than the goal match enhancement for all participants

span.label: The two hippocampal signals divide by content: match enhancement tracks the match to the maintained goal while mismatch enhancement tracks perceptual mismatch, dissociating components of working memory within the hippocampus.
span.quote: The dissociation of different components of working memory at hippocampus revealed more information beyond previous electrophysiological research [ 18 , 19 ], demonstrating that match enhancement is more related with goal match at the hippocampus and mismatch enhancement is more related with perceptual mismatch.

span.label: Participants whose right posterior hippocampus produced a later perceptual mismatch enhancement were more accurate, a positive correlation between latency and memory performance.
span.quote: The accuracy was found to be positively correlated with the perceptual mismatch enhancement latency on the right posterior hippocampus.

span.label: That latency-accuracy link is read as evidence that the right posterior hippocampal mismatch latency indexes the quality of memory retrieval.
span.quote: This suggested that the latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement at the right posterior hippocampus could indicate the performance of memory retrieval.

span.label: In six of the eight patients, single-trial intracranial field potentials from the right hippocampus were sufficient to classify whether the trial was a match task or a switch task.
span.quote: Six out of 8 participants showed that the task demand could be decoded from the IFP response on the right hippocampus.

span.label: Behaviourally, responses were faster in the match task than in the switch task.
span.quote: Paired sample t tests revealed that the responses in the match task were faster than those in the switch task

span.label: Hippocampal engagement here is attributed to the task requiring object identity and location to be bound together, in both the match and the switch task.
span.quote: Our results agree with these studies, in that object and location information are combined to finish the task requirements, no matter whether it is in a match task trial or a switch task trial.

span.label: goal match enhancement appeared in the left posterior hippocampus between about 520 and 735 ms after probe onset
span.quote: Two similar time intervals were found (535 ms to 735 ms on electrode contact #3, and 520 ms to 590 ms on electrode contact #4) to be significant (Fig. 3 ).

span.label: perceptual mismatch enhancement appeared bilaterally in anterior and posterior hippocampus, averaging 376 to 555 ms
span.quote: A perceptually driven mismatch enhancement was revealed bilaterally in the hippocampus including both the anterior and posterior areas (electrode contacts #1, #2, #3, #4 and #9, #10, #11, #12). This enhancement effect occurred at different intervals on different electrode contacts, averaging from 376 ms to 555 ms (Fig. 4 ).

span.label: mismatch preceded match in every participant, by about 150 ms
span.quote: The perceptual mismatch enhancement began earlier than the goal match enhancement for all participants (latency of match enhancement vs latency of mismatch enhancement in left posterior hippocampus: t (7) = 2.43, P < 0.05).

span.label: region latencies were 524 ms for goal match and about 405 to 430 ms for perceptual mismatch across the four subdivisions
span.quote: The goal match enhancement was found in the left posterior hippocampus with a latency of 524 ms. The latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement varied across areas: left anterior 411 ms, left posterior 405 ms, right anterior 430 ms, and right posterior 409 ms.

span.label: a late perceptual match effect appeared on two electrodes at 717 and 900 ms, fitting neither canonical pattern
span.quote: A late perceptual match enhancement was found on electrodes #2 and #3 with a latency of 717 ms and 900 ms, which fitted a pattern of BOTH > NEITHER and GOAL < PERCEPT.

span.label: every observed latency survived a 1000-permutation test at p below 0.05
span.quote: For each electrode and each significant effect, the probability of the observed latency was <0.05.

span.label: mismatch latency in the right posterior hippocampus correlated positively with memory accuracy
span.quote: The latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement effect found in the right posterior hippocampus was significantly correlated with the accuracy of memory performance (Fig. 5 ) (ρ = 0.74, P < 0.05).

span.label: task demand was decodable from single trials in 6 of 8 patients, always from the right hippocampus
span.quote: With the TTL 2 datasets, 6 out of 8 patients consistently showed a significantly reliable response in the hippocampus representing the task demand. More interestingly, we found that for all 6 patients, the IFP signal in the right hippocampus efficiently discriminated the task demand (Table 3 ).

span.label: responses were faster in the match task than in the switch task
span.quote: Paired sample t tests revealed that the responses in the match task were faster than those in the switch task ( t (7) = −3.608, P < 0.01).

span.label: over 80% of trials survived artifact rejection
span.quote: We managed to retain >80% of all trials after artifact rejection.

span.label: match enhancement and mismatch enhancement
span.quote: Emerging evidence has revealed that, within the hippocampus, neurons discriminate between novel and familiar stimuli through a firing rate increase to previously encountered stimuli (match enhancement), or through a firing rate increase to novel stimuli (mismatch enhancement) [ 17 – 19 ].

span.label: modified delayed-match-to-sample paradigm that separates goal match from perceptual match
span.term: modified delayed-match-to-sample paradigm that separates goal match from perceptual match
span.quote: This paradigm dissociates goal match/mismatch from perceptual match/mismatch.

span.label: BOTH, NEITHER, GOAL and PERCEPT probe conditions
span.term: BOTH, NEITHER, GOAL and PERCEPT probe conditions
span.quote: 1, the same objects at the same locations, called BOTH in the match task (correct response for this trial is ‘yes’) or PERCEPT in the switch task (correct response is ‘no’); 2, the same objects but switched locations, called NEITHER in the match task (correct response is ‘no’) or GOAL in the switch task (correct response is ‘yes’)

span.label: latency of the enhancement effect (operational definition)
span.term: latency of the enhancement effect (operational definition)
span.quote: The latency of the enhancement effect for the individual participant was defined in an interval when the GOAL condition was significantly larger than the PERCEPT condition, and then as the time point when the BOTH and NEITHER conditions that fitted the two enhancement patterns started to be significant.

span.label: match enhancement
span.quote: Emerging evidence has revealed that, within the hippocampus, neurons discriminate between novel and familiar stimuli through a firing rate increase to previously encountered stimuli (match enhancement), or through a firing rate increase to novel stimuli (mismatch enhancement)

span.label: delayed-match-to-sample
span.quote: A modified version of the delayed-match-to-sample task was used. This paradigm dissociates goal match/mismatch from perceptual match/mismatch.

span.label: intracranial field potential
span.quote: We used a statistical learning approach [ 34 ] to quantify whether the information from IFPs available in single trials was sufficient to distinguish whether it is memory maintenance (match task) or simulation of a specific future event (switch task).

span.label: task instruction (match task versus switch task)
span.term: task instruction (match task versus switch task)
span.quote: If the trial was a match task, the participant was required to discriminate whether the identity and location of the two probe objects was exactly the same as the sample objects.

span.label: probe object configuration (four possible identity/location arrangements)
span.term: probe object configuration (four possible identity/location arrangements)
span.quote: Thus, there were 4 possible object configurations in the Probe display

span.label: event-related potential amplitude per stimulus condition
span.term: event-related potential amplitude per stimulus condition
span.quote: The absolute values of ERPs for correct trials were averaged for each stimulus condition.

span.label: local field potential difference across conditions over time
span.term: local field potential difference across conditions over time
span.quote: The sample-by-sample t -test gave a time-resolved significance level for whether the local field potential (LFP) values differed across conditions.

span.label: latency of the goal match / perceptual mismatch enhancement
span.term: latency of the goal match / perceptual mismatch enhancement
span.quote: The latency of the enhancement effect for the individual participant was defined in an interval when the GOAL condition was significantly larger than the PERCEPT condition, and then as the time point when the BOTH and NEITHER conditions that fitted the two enhancement patterns started to be significant.

span.label: reaction time and accuracy
span.quote: Behavioral performance measured by mean reaction time and accuracy.

span.label: LOC and OBJ probe conditions
span.quote: The last two conditions were designed for control purposes.

span.label: electrode configuration (identical implantation scheme and contact order in every patient)
span.term: electrode configuration (identical implantation scheme and contact order in every patient)
span.quote: This electrode configuration was used for every patient and allowed us to collect neuronal response data from the same (or at least similar) brain region, with the same electrode order across patients, making grand average of event-related potentials (ERPs) possible [ 30 ].

span.label: trial correctness (only correct trials entered the ERP analyses)
span.term: trial correctness (only correct trials entered the ERP analyses)
span.quote: Only correct trials were used in the following ERP analyses.

span.label: latency
span.quote: The goal match enhancement was found in the left posterior hippocampus with a latency of 524 ms. The latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement varied across areas: left anterior 411 ms, left posterior 405 ms, right anterior 430 ms, and right posterior 409 ms.

span.label: task demand
span.quote: We used a statistical learning approach [ 34 ] to quantify whether the information from IFPs available in single trials was sufficient to distinguish whether it is memory maintenance (match task) or simulation of a specific future event (switch task).

span.label: correct percentage
span.quote: The latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement effect found in the right posterior hippocampus was significantly correlated with the accuracy of memory performance (Fig. 5 ) (ρ = 0.74, P < 0.05).

span.label: 120 ... 8 — depth electrode contacts recorded, and epilepsy patients implanted
span.quote: Intracranial field potentials were recorded from 120 depth electrode contacts implanted in 8 human epilepsy patients who suffered from pharmaco-resistant epilepsy in Xuanwu Hospital (5 male, 3 female).

span.label: 126 — trials per experimental run
span.quote: The experiment was arranged in separate runs composed of 126 trials.

span.label: >80% — proportion of trials retained after artifact rejection
span.quote: We managed to retain >80% of all trials after artifact rejection.

span.label: 1000 — random permutations computed per electrode to test the observed enhancement latencies
span.quote: For each electrode showing a significant effect, we computed 1000 random permutations of the observed effects in the four conditions with data pooled from all electrodes; for each permutation, we then conducted the same two-step t -test analysis to get a significant latency.

span.label: <0.05 — permutation probability of the observed latency, for every electrode and every significant effect
span.quote: For each electrode and each significant effect, the probability of the observed latency was <0.05.

span.label: 6 out of 8 — patients whose hippocampal field potentials reliably represented the task demand in single-trial decoding
span.quote: Six out of 8 participants showed that the task demand could be decoded from the IFP response on the right hippocampus.

span.label: 120 depth electrode contacts in 8 patients — the sample
span.quote: Intracranial field potentials were recorded from 120 depth electrode contacts implanted in 8 human epilepsy patients who suffered from pharmaco-resistant epilepsy in Xuanwu Hospital (5 male, 3 female).

span.label: 520 ms to 735 ms — window of goal match enhancement after probe onset
span.quote: We also found that this effect happened within 520 ms to 735 ms after the probe onset, ~150 ms later than the perceptual mismatch enhancement found bilaterally in both the anterior and posterior hippocampus.

span.label: 376 ms to 555 ms — window of perceptual mismatch enhancement
span.quote: A perceptually driven mismatch enhancement was revealed bilaterally in the hippocampus including both the anterior and posterior areas (electrode contacts #1, #2, #3, #4 and #9, #10, #11, #12). This enhancement effect occurred at different intervals on different electrode contacts, averaging from 376 ms to 555 ms (Fig. 4 ).

span.label: ~150 ms — how much earlier mismatch precedes match
span.quote: We also found that this effect happened within 520 ms to 735 ms after the probe onset, ~150 ms later than the perceptual mismatch enhancement found bilaterally in both the anterior and posterior hippocampus.

span.label: ρ = 0.74 — correlation between right posterior mismatch latency and accuracy
span.quote: The latency of the perceptual mismatch enhancement effect found in the right posterior hippocampus was significantly correlated with the accuracy of memory performance (Fig. 5 ) (ρ = 0.74, P < 0.05).

span.label: 126 trials per run, 3 to 5 runs — to obtain at least 80 correct trials per participant
span.quote: The experiment was arranged in separate runs composed of 126 trials. Each individual participated in 3 to 5 runs, depending on performance, in order to obtain no less than 80 [ 33 ] correct trials.

span.label: 6 out of 8 — patients whose task demand was decodable from hippocampal signal
span.quote: With the TTL 2 datasets, 6 out of 8 patients consistently showed a significantly reliable response in the hippocampus representing the task demand. More interestingly, we found that for all 6 patients, the IFP signal in the right hippocampus efficiently discriminated the task demand (Table 3 ).
